title: The Python Iterator Protocol and StopIteration
learningObjectives: Explain the main ideas in the python iterator protocol and stopiteration.
Use the relevant iterator or generator protocol correctly.
Trace values and state across successive iteration steps.
Recognize exhaustion, lazy evaluation and relevant edge cases.
Apply the concept to a practical sequence-processing task.

understand.concept: The iterator protocol requires __iter__() to return an iterator and __next__() to return the next value or raise StopIteration. A well-behaved iterator returns itself from __iter__(). StopIteration is the defined end-of-iteration signal, not an ordinary error to leak from a loop body.
understand.whyItMatters: Understanding the protocol helps developers create interoperable data sources and diagnose iteration bugs in custom classes and libraries.
understand.analogy: The protocol is like an agreed interface between a dispenser and a person collecting items: one operation provides the dispenser, and another advances it.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not cover Python's special-method lookup rules, generator semantics or resource cleanup. Custom iterators must also consider re-entrancy and whether they are reusable.

explain.narrative:
## Two special methods
An iterator implements `__iter__()` and `__next__()`. The `__iter__()` method returns the iterator itself. The `__next__()` method returns the next available item. When no item remains, it raises `StopIteration` rather than returning a sentinel that could also be valid data.

## Why StopIteration matters
Python's iteration machinery recognizes StopIteration as normal completion. A for loop catches this signal and exits. A custom iterator should raise it only when the sequence is exhausted. Do not use `return None` to signal completion if None could be a legitimate item.

## Robust protocol design
Define exactly when the iterator is exhausted and keep its state consistent. If the iterator owns external resources, design a separate context-management or close mechanism; iteration completion alone is not a universal resource-cleanup guarantee.

examples.title: Check that iter returns the iterator
examples.explanation: An iterator's __iter__ method returns the iterator object itself.

examples.title: Catch StopIteration explicitly
examples.explanation: The second next call signals normal exhaustion with StopIteration.

examples.title: Use a default instead of try/except
examples.code:
it = iter([])
value = next(it, None)
print(value is None)
examples.explanation: A default avoids an exception when the iterator is empty, provided the default is distinguishable from valid values.

examples.title: None can be a real iterator item
examples.explanation: Returning None is not the iterator completion protocol; StopIteration is the dedicated signal.

examples.title: A loop ends on StopIteration
examples.explanation: The for statement handles StopIteration internally and continues after the loop.

practise.guidedTask: Write a small program that demonstrates the python iterator protocol and stopiteration. Show at least two iteration steps and explain how the state changes.
practise.independentTask: Build a reusable or one-pass sequence processor using this topic. Test normal input, an empty or exhausted case, and describe when each value is calculated.
hints: Identify whether the object is an iterable, an iterator or both.

Choose a list only when repeated access or storage is required.
practise.challenge: Process a larger sequence incrementally and compare the memory and reuse trade-offs with building a list first.

questions.prompt: What should __iter__() return on an iterator object?
questions.explanation: The iterator protocol requires an iterator's __iter__ method to return itself.

questions.prompt: What should __next__() do when no values remain?
questions.explanation: StopIteration is the protocol-defined signal for normal iteration completion.

questions.prompt: Why is None not a reliable universal end marker?
questions.answer: None may be a valid item
options: None may be a valid item
None is not a Python object
None is always false in a loop
questions.explanation: An iterator may legitimately contain None, so exhaustion needs its own signal.
__next__ returns and advances to the next item.

questions.prompt: Does a for loop normally expose StopIteration to the loop body?
questions.answer: No, it handles the signal and ends the loop
options: No, it handles the signal and ends the loop
Only when the loop uses break
questions.explanation: The for statement manages iterator exhaustion internally.
